pros: Finds shortest path in unweighted graphs (minimum number of edges)
Simple to implement with a queue (few lines of code)
Guaranteed to find target if it exists (complete for finite graphs)
Explores nodes in order of distance (natural for level-based analysis)
Can be used for cycle detection and bipartite graph testing
Foundation for more complex algorithms (Dijkstra, Prim, Edmonds-Karp)
Easily modified for bidirectional search (dramatic speedup)
Works on both directed and undirected graphs
Can compute distances for ALL reachable nodes from source
O(V+E) complexity is optimal for graph traversal
Multi-source BFS extends naturally for multiple starting points
cons: O(V) memory for queue (problematic for very large graphs)
Not suitable for weighted graphs (use Dijkstra instead)
Does not consider edge costs or weights
Single-source: must rerun for different sources
May explore entire connected component before finding target
Inefficient for deep graphs (exponential frontier growth)
Queue can grow large in wide graphs (e.g., social networks)
Cannot handle dynamic graphs during traversal
Recursive DFS may be simpler for some applications (e.g., topological sort)
Does not record multiple shortest paths without modification
